Courses/Mobile system design, from a packet to an app

Practice chapter 2 of 2

Measure what happened on real devices

  1. Give crash and unresponsive rates a denominator
  2. Spend a network error budget on a user journey
  3. Connect a slow screen to searchable events
  4. Read the tail without discarding the average

Give crash and unresponsive rates a denominator

A crash ends a process abnormally; an application-not-responding event captures a failure to respond under platform conditions. Define whether you count events, affected users, sessions or operations and over which interval. Platform vitals have specific user-based definitions. Avoid comparing them directly to an independently defined per-request rate.

Worked example

In a fictional day 100 users open the app. One user crashes five times and another crashes once. The affected-user fraction is 2%, while the raw event count is six. If one of those users also experiences an unresponsive screen, summing separate affected-user counts double-counts that person.

Try it

A release with fewer overall users has fewer total crashes. What would make a comparison informative?

Compare your answer

Compare equivalent affected-user measures over the same window, with cohort sizes, version, device mix and uncertainty visible. Inspect the new stack or trace grouping as well as the aggregate.

Source · Android Developers · Android vitals

Spend a network error budget on a user journey

A service-level indicator is an observed fraction, such as completed feed refreshes divided by eligible refreshes. A service-level objective sets its target over a window. The error budget is the permitted shortfall. Decide what counts as good when offline reading works but refreshing fails, and avoid counting each transport retry as an independent user journey.

Worked example

A target of 99.5% successful refreshes across 20,000 attempts allows 100 unsuccessful journeys. If 70 have failed, 30 remain. Five hundred failed low-level calls could represent fewer failed refreshes if retries eventually completed within the deadline. Track both layers with separate names.

Try it

If 40 of the next already-budgeted journeys fail, what has happened to the original allowance?

Compare your answer

There are now 110 failures against the fixed 100 allowance, ten beyond it. For a rolling window, recalculate numerator and denominator as older events leave and new ones arrive.

Source · Google SRE · Implementing SLOs

Connect a slow screen to searchable events

Emit structured observations with stable fields for operation, app version, outcome and elapsed time. Use a correlation or trace ID to follow one refresh through the phone and server when available. Prefer an operation name to a full URL containing user data. Keep credentials and private content out of diagnostic events.

Worked example

An event for feed.refresh has outcome timeout, version 14, elapsed 1,980 ms and a trace ID. The server trace shows a 90 ms handler after the request arrived. Inspect client queueing, connectivity, network transit and rendering; the difference does not automatically belong to any single stage.

Try it

Two logs contain the same bookmark title. Is that reliable evidence that they belong to one refresh?

Compare your answer

No. Different users and retries can produce identical titles. Use a generated request or trace identity with a clear retry relationship. Query by structured fields without copying user content into logs.

Source · OpenTelemetry · Logs Data Model

Read the tail without discarding the average

A percentile is a position in ordered observations. For nearest-rank p99 of 100 successful requests, inspect position 99. A mean describes total duration divided by count; the tail describes a different experience. State whether timeouts and failed requests are excluded and report their frequency separately.

Worked example

Ninety-eight requests take 100 ms and two take 2,000 ms. The mean is (9,800 + 4,000) / 100 = 138 ms. Position 99 is 2,000 ms. A change that improves the fast requests can lower the mean while leaving both very slow users unaffected.

Try it

Can you average the p99 from a small Wi-Fi cohort and a large cellular cohort to get the overall p99?

Compare your answer

No. Combine underlying observations or compatible histograms weighted by their actual counts and compute the percentile again. Keep cohort-level tails too, because a small affected population can disappear in the aggregate.

Source · Google SRE · Monitoring distributed systems
